title: Akiva and Rachel (Ketubot 62b–63a)
hookLine: his wife sends him to study for years; he tells his students that all they have is hers

cards: Watch the end of any awards show. Someone holds up a statue and thanks their spouse, their mom, the teacher who stayed late. Sometimes it's a line.
Sometimes you can tell the person in the audience gave up years for this. Behind a lot of big stories there's somebody who isn't on stage.
Yesterday's telling of Akiva's beginning, the man and the stone, comes from Avot de-Rabbi Natan. The Talmud tells it another way: through the woman who believed in him before anyone else did.

teach.b: In tractate Ketubot, Akiva is a shepherd working for Kalba Savua, a very rich man. The rich man's daughter sees something in him: he's modest and good.
She asks: if I marry you, will you go and study? He says yes. They marry quietly, and her father, furious, cuts her off without a penny.
Akiva goes away to study for twelve years. Coming home, he hears an old man mocking her outside the house: how long will you live like a widow with a living husband?

And she answers: if he listened to me, he'd stay away another twelve. So he turns around, without even going in, and studies twelve more. When he finally returns, twenty-four thousand students walk with him.
His wife goes out to meet him and falls at his feet. The students don't know who she is, and start to push her away. Akiva stops them.
What is mine and what is yours is hers. Everything I know, and everything I've taught you, belongs to her. Parts of this story are hard to hear today: years apart, poverty, a father's anger.
The Talmud doesn't hide them. But its last word is gratitude, said out loud, in front of everyone.

how: The story of Akiva and Rachel is often retold in Jewish classes as a picture of a partnership built on learning, and of saying thank you in public.

o: Akiva's mother, who raised him as a shepherd
a teacher who taught Akiva the alphabet at forty
the wife who sent Akiva off to study for years

games.q: who did what in Ketubot — tap the pairs.
p: the rich father who cut her off
studied twelve years, then twelve more

s: Akiva came home after twelve years and stayed
he heard her say he should study twelve more, and went back.
the Talmud's text names her Rachel
Ketubot calls her Kalba Savua's daughter; tradition knows her as Rachel.
Akiva told his students everything they had was hers
what is mine and what is yours is hers.

games.q: you're Akiva, back after twelve years. outside the door you hear her say she'd gladly wait twelve more. what do you do?
o: go in. twelve years is enough.
turn around and study twelve more.
take her with you this time.
games.why: he turned around without going in, and came back twelve years later with twenty-four thousand students.

practice: Think of something you're proud of, a skill, a job, a child you've raised, a hard year you got through, and look behind it: who made room for it, covered for you, drove you, fed you, believed in you before there was any reason to?
Let one face come, and stay with them. If you had the microphone, what would you say?

wordCard.voice: Rachel, who sent her husband Akiva to study for years, and stood firm when he was mocked for it. When he came back with thousands of students, he said: what is mine and yours is hers.

orig.note: Hebrew, Ketubot 63a: mine and yours, it is hers.

carryVoice: Your line: what is mine is hers. Behind twenty-four thousand students stood one woman. See you tomorrow.
